title.title: Limitations & Risks
title.subtitle: The oracle problem, technical limits, and where smart contracts fall short

oracle.heading: The oracle problem, now as a risk
oracle.subtitle: You have seen why contracts need oracles and how a feed gets bent. Here it goes on the risk register.

links.label: Data source
links.guard: One sensor, one API, one market

links.label: Oracle
links.guard: A few to a few dozen nodes

oracle.chainNote: The chain secures the contract. Nothing on-chain secures the number it acts on, so the system is only as strong as its weakest link.
oracle.askLabel: Three questions for any contract that reads outside data

asks.a: One operator or one source is a single point of failure.

asks.q: What if it is late or wrong?
asks.a: The contract acts on it anyway. It cannot tell the difference.

asks.q: What would it cost to bend it?
asks.a: If that is less than the money the number controls, expect an attack.

oracle.limit: better oracles shrink this risk. None removes it.

reading.label: Further reading
reading.note: A systematisation of oracle designs, the attacks on them and the mitigations.

challenges.heading: Challenges & Limitations
challenges.subtitle: Smart contracts inherit their chain's constraints. Four of them shape every design decision.

items.title: Throughput
items.what: L1 can't match Web2 volume
items.why: Every node re-executes every transaction, so base-layer throughput stays low.
items.fix: L2 rollups reach thousands of TPS and still settle on L1.

items.title: Latency
items.what: Block times vs the millisecond web
items.why: A transaction waits for the next block, then for confirmations, before it is safe to rely on.
items.fix: An L2 confirms in about 250 ms and settles on L1 underneath.

items.title: Storage Cost
items.what: On-chain storage is very expensive
items.why: Every full node keeps the data forever, so the protocol prices storage to discourage bloat.
items.fix: Keep only a hash on-chain; put the data on IPFS or Arweave.
items.web: Cloud: cents per GB a month

items.title: Computation Limits
items.what: Gas caps what a transaction can compute
items.why: Each block has a hard gas ceiling, so ML inference or heavy loops cannot run on-chain.
items.fix: Compute off-chain; post the result with a ZK proof the chain can verify.

technical.heading: Technical Challenges & Limitations
technical.subtitle: Four structural problems: what they are, why they happen, and how the field is fixing them.

items.title: MEV — Maximal Extractable Value
items.what: Block producers reorder transactions for profit
items.why: They choose which transactions go in and in what order, so they can front-run or sandwich a trade waiting in the mempool.
items.fix: Private transaction routing (Flashbots Protect), commit-reveal, batch-auction DEXs (CoW Protocol).

items.title: Upgradability
items.what: Immutable code can't be patched
items.why: A critical bug stays exploitable. The DAO lost $60M and forced an Ethereum hard fork.
items.fix: Audit before deploy; add an upgrade proxy only if essential, behind a timelock and a multisig.
items.stat: The proxy's admin key is a new centralisation point → Admin Keys

items.title: The Blockchain Trilemma
items.what: Security · scalability · decentralisation — pick 2
items.why: Maximising all three at L1 isn't possible; every chain deliberately trades one away.
items.fix: Ethereum keeps security + decentralisation and pushes scale to L2 rollups.

items.title: State Growth
items.what: The chain only ever grows
items.why: History is append-only and full nodes keep it, so running one drifts toward datacenter hardware.
items.fix: History expiry (EIP-4444) and stateless clients cut what a node must store.
items.stat: Ethereum full node: 1 TB+ · archive node: many TB

exercise.title: Defend the Oracle
exercise.subtitle: A crop-insurance contract pays $5,000 if June rainfall is under 50 mm. You know how a feed gets attacked. For each weak point, decide what you would change, then check what the defence still leaves exposed.

items.title: One data source
items.desc: Every reading comes from one weather station. Whoever can touch the station can move the payout.
items.defenceDesc: Cross-check the weather service, satellite data and local stations; discard outliers.
items.residual: Sources disagree. Someone must define which one counts, and that definition becomes the target.

items.title: One operator
items.desc: A single company runs the only weather oracle. Hack it, bribe it or unplug it, and the contract follows.
items.defenceDesc: Many independent nodes report; the contract takes the median.
items.residual: Costs more per update, and the nodes may all be reading the same upstream source.

items.title: Any value, any age
items.desc: The contract accepts whatever arrives: last week's reading, or 0 mm in the middle of a storm.
items.defenceDesc: Reject stale timestamps and out-of-range values; pause payouts when the feed looks wrong.
items.residual: A pause freezes honest claims too, and whoever holds the pause switch is a new trusted party (see Admin Keys).

items.title: Instant, final payout
items.desc: The contract pays the moment the number lands. There is no appeal and no reversal.
items.defenceDesc: Hold the payout for 24 hours so anyone can challenge the reading (the optimistic-oracle model).
items.residual: Slower payouts, somebody has to be watching, and a dispute still needs a judge.

exercise.verdict: every defence moves the trust somewhere else or puts a price on it. None deletes it.

security.heading: Security Risks
security.subtitle: Bugs are public, permanent, and exploited within hours. The most expensive ones are the simplest.

items.title: Reentrancy
items.what: Calls out before updating its own state — attacker calls back in and drains it.

items.title: Flash Loan Attacks
items.what: The Section 2 price attack: borrow millions with no collateral, bend a spot price, cash in, repay. One transaction.

items.title: Access Control
items.what: Critical functions (mint, withdraw, upgrade) miss the right modifier.

items.title: Over/Underflow
items.what: Pre-0.8 Solidity wraps silently — balance − x underflows to a huge number.

items.title: Logic Bugs
items.what: Code runs as written, but the logic is wrong — off-by-one, bad sign, wrong arg.
items.stat: Tools miss these — humans catch them

total.title: Cumulative Loss
total.what: Thousands of incidents — usually a missing modifier or a copy-paste slip.
total.fix: Audits are a discipline, not a checkbox

cost.heading: Cost Risks
cost.subtitle: Budget for the upfront and the ongoing costs.

phases.ongoingNote: after launch, for as long as it runs

items.title: Immutability & Redeployment
items.what: You can't patch — you redeploy
items.why: A fix means a new contract plus migrating users and state. Ship-and-iterate does not apply.
items.fix: Test hard before launch; plan the v1→v2 migration path up front.

items.title: Development & Maintenance
items.what: Scarce, expensive expertise
items.why: Solidity expertise is scarce, and even strong developers ship bugs they cannot hot-fix.
items.fix: Budget auditors and security engineers as a line item, not an afterthought.

items.title: Gas & Execution
items.what: Fees vary and compound
items.why: Fees spike 10–100× under congestion, and inefficient code taxes every future user.
items.fix: Optimise storage writes and external calls; reconsider micro-payment economics.

items.title: Security vs Performance
items.what: Every safety check costs gas
items.why: Defensive checks trade off against efficiency, and audit cost scales with code complexity.
items.fix: A ~$50K audit per ~500 lines is normal; bug bounties add cost but cut catastrophic risk.

regulatory.heading: Regulatory Risks
regulatory.subtitle: Code and law overlap, and the law has not caught up.

items.title: Legal Adjudication
items.what: May not count as a valid contract
items.code: Executes automatically, often with no signatures and no mutual assent.
items.law: A court may not treat it as a contract, so enforcement is uncertain.
items.note: "Code is law" gets overruled when stakes are high (The DAO fork).
items.tag: Pair on-chain logic with a legal wrapper

items.title: Privacy vs Transparency
items.what: Public by design clashes with GDPR
items.code: Every transaction is visible to all nodes.
items.law: The right to be forgotten (GDPR) and health-data privacy (HIPAA).
items.note: Even hashes leak via metadata and linkability.
items.tag: ZK proofs · permissioned chains · off-chain encryption

items.title: Tech Outpaces Law
items.what: Rules lag the technology by years
items.note: A contract legal in Singapore may be illegal in the US.
items.tag: EU's MiCA (2024) is the first comprehensive exception

quiz.question: A DeFi lending protocol uses a single on-chain DEX spot price as its collateral oracle. An attacker takes a $50M flash loan, manipulates the DEX price, borrows against inflated collateral, and repays the loan — all in one transaction. Which property of flash loans makes this different from ordinary market manipulation?
options: Flash loans are anonymous — the attacker cannot be traced or prosecuted.
Flash loans need no upfront capital — borrow, attack and repay happen in one atomic transaction, so the attacker risks only the gas fee.
Flash loans exploit a bug in the Ethereum protocol itself, making them impossible to prevent at the contract level.
Flash loans allow attackers to bypass gas fees, making the attack economically viable even for small protocols.
quiz.explanation: The loan is borrowed, used and repaid inside one atomic transaction that reverts if any step fails, so the attacker needs no capital and risks only gas. A TWAP or a multi-source oracle is far harder to move within one transaction.

adminKey.question: A protocol advertises "immutable, audited smart contracts". Its contracts sit behind an upgradeable proxy controlled by one key, with no timelock. What is the most accurate risk assessment?
options: Low risk: the audit also covers any future version of the logic.
Low risk: a proxy only forwards calls, so it cannot change how funds are handled.
Whoever holds that key can swap the logic at any moment, so users are trusting the key holder and not only the audited code.
The only downside is that calls through a proxy cost slightly more gas.
adminKey.explanation: An audit covers the version that was reviewed, not the one an admin installs tomorrow; with one key and no timelock, the rules can change instantly and users get no time to leave.

pattern.question: Ronin ($625M), Beanstalk ($182M), Mango Markets ($114M) and Terra (~$40B) are four of the largest losses in the field. What do they have in common?
options: The contract code largely did what it was written to do; the failure was in keys, governance, price data or economic design.
All four were reentrancy bugs of the kind that drained The DAO.
All four were caused by integer overflow in pre-0.8 Solidity.
All four exploited a flaw in Ethereum's consensus protocol.
pattern.explanation: Stolen keys (Ronin), a flash-loaned vote (Beanstalk), a manipulated price (Mango) and an economic design that ran on belief (Terra): none needed a classic coding bug, so a code audit alone would not have caught them.

sameSource.question: A crop-insurance contract replaces its single weather oracle with a network of 21 independent nodes and takes the median. All 21 nodes read the same weather API. What has the change achieved?
options: Oracle risk is gone: a majority of the 21 nodes would now have to collude.
Nothing: a decentralised oracle network adds cost and no security.
The chain's validators now check the rainfall figure before it is used.
No single operator can bend the number, but one wrong API value still passes the median untouched.
sameSource.explanation: A median protects against a lying node, not a lying source: the trust has moved from the operator to the one upstream API.

proxyGuard.question: A team wants to keep the ability to fix bugs through its upgradeable proxy. Which change most reduces the risk to users?
options: Renounce the admin key, so that nobody can ever change the logic again.
Put upgrades behind a multisig and a timelock, so no single key can act and users get notice.
Commission a second audit of the logic contract that is currently live.
Move the single admin key to a hardware wallet held by the CEO.
proxyGuard.explanation: A multisig removes the single key and a timelock gives users time to leave; renouncing ends upgrades altogether, and an audit says nothing about the next version.

budget.question: A team budgets for building a contract and assumes it can fix problems after launch, as it would with a web app. Which cost is it most likely underestimating?
options: Audits before launch, plus a redeploy and user migration if a bug ever appears.
The deployment transaction itself, which is usually the largest single cost of a project.
Server bills for the nodes that run the contract, which the team pays every month.
Per-user licence fees for the Solidity compiler and the EVM.
budget.explanation: Deployed code cannot be patched, so deployment is the cheap part: audits (about $50K per ~500 lines) and any redeploy-and-migrate are the real budget.

erasure.question: A health app writes patients' personal data directly to a public blockchain. A patient later invokes the GDPR right to be forgotten. What is the core problem?
options: None: addresses are pseudonymous, so data-protection law does not apply.
None: the contract's admin can delete the patient's records from the chain.
The data sits on every node and cannot be erased, so the request cannot be honoured.
Only the gas cost: erasing data on-chain is possible but expensive.
erasure.explanation: Public and permanent by design collides with the right to be forgotten, which is why personal data belongs off-chain.

audited.question: Euler Finance had been audited, yet in March 2023 one missing check in a single function cost $197M. Which conclusion does the incident best support?
options: Audits add no real security, so a team can safely skip them.
The loss came from stolen admin keys, which no audit can cover.
Formal verification would have made the contract provably free of all bugs.
Audits lower the odds of a bug but cannot rule one out, so plan for the incident too.
audited.explanation: The bug slipped past review: audits reduce risk, they do not remove it, so plan for the incident and not only for prevention.

takeaways.title: Section 05 — Key Takeaways
items: Oracle risk (Section 2) never goes away: defences move the trust or put a price on it, they do not delete it
Immutability cuts both ways: bugs are permanent, and upgrade proxies trade that for trust in an admin key
"Code is law" means users have no recourse when code behaves correctly but harmfully
Throughput, latency, storage and gas limits make a database the faster, cheaper choice in many contexts
Keys, votes, oracles and economic design fail as often as code; Ronin, Beanstalk, Mango and Terra lost ~$41B without a bug in the contract logic
Audits are the entry ticket, not a guarantee; $6B+ lost since 2016
Regulatory uncertainty: laws move in years, contracts move in months — privacy, enforceability, and jurisdiction all matter

adminKey.heading: Admin Keys and Upgradeable Proxies
adminKey.subtitle: How "immutable" contracts get changed, and who is allowed to do it.

diagram.proxyNote: fixed address · holds the funds and data · forwards every call to the current logic
diagram.adminNote: whoever holds it can point the proxy at new rules

points.title: What it is
points.desc: A proxy is a fixed front door that forwards calls to a separate logic contract. The admin key is the permission to change which logic the door points to.

points.title: Why it exists
points.desc: Deployed code cannot be patched. Teams add a proxy so they can fix bugs and ship features without asking every user to move.

points.title: Why it matters to you
points.desc: The key holder can change the rules, pause the contract or move the funds. The trust you removed from a bank now sits with whoever holds that key.

adminKey.askLabel: Before relying on a contract, ask:

failures.heading: When it went wrong — six real incidents
failures.subtitle: Each maps to one risk from this section. In most, the contract did exactly what it was told.
failures.codeOk: The code did what it was told
failures.tally: {{n}} of {{total}}: the code did what it was told
failures.footer: Keys, votes, data feeds and economic design fail at least as often as the code. Security is a property of the whole system.

items.name: Ronin Bridge (Axie Infinity)
items.what: The bridge needed 5 of 9 validator signatures. Attackers obtained five keys through social engineering — four run by one company — and withdrew everything.
items.lesson: A multisig is only as decentralised as the people holding the keys.

items.name: Beanstalk
items.what: An attacker flash-loaned enough tokens to hold 67% of the votes, passed a proposal that sent the treasury to themselves, and repaid the loan — in one transaction.
items.lesson: On-chain voting without a timelock turns governance itself into an attack surface.

items.name: Mango Markets
items.what: The Section 2 price attack with real money: the attacker pumped thinly traded MNGO on the exchanges feeding Mango's price oracle, borrowed against the inflated collateral and left.
items.lesson: If your price comes from one shallow market, the oracle is the vault door.

items.name: Euler Finance
items.what: A single missing health check in a donate function let a flash-loan attacker create bad debt and liquidate it for profit. Audited — the bug slipped through. Most funds were later returned.
items.lesson: Audits reduce risk; they do not remove it. Plan for the incident, not just the prevention.

items.name: Parity multisig wallet
items.what: A user accidentally took ownership of a shared library contract and then destroyed it. Every wallet built on it froze — permanently. The funds are still there, unreachable.
items.lesson: Immutability means a mistake is forever. Who can call what must be designed, not assumed.

items.name: Terra / UST
items.what: The algorithmic stablecoin held its peg only while people believed it would. A large sell-off broke the peg; the sister token minted to defend it collapsed to zero within days.
items.lesson: The code worked as designed. The design was the flaw — a risk no audit can catch.

keyPoints.s5-oracle: Oracle risk can be reduced and priced, never removed: treat the data feed like any other counterparty.
keyPoints.s5-challenges: Slow, expensive, public and permanent: every design decision trades against one of these.
keyPoints.s5-technical: The fixes exist, but each one reintroduces a party you must trust.
keyPoints.s5-ex-oracle: Every oracle defence moves the trust somewhere else; know where it went.
keyPoints.s5-risks-security: Bugs are public, permanent and exploited within hours; an audit is the entry ticket.
keyPoints.s5-admin-key: An upgradeable contract is only as trustworthy as the holder of its admin key; ask who holds it and what limits them.
keyPoints.s5-failures: In most incidents the contract did what it was told; the failure was in the design, the data or the people.
keyPoints.s5-risks-cost: The cheap part is the deployment; audits, monitoring, upgrades and gas during peaks are the real budget.
keyPoints.s5-risks-regulatory: When code and law disagree, the law wins; plan for jurisdiction, data protection and liability.
